processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The steel used in this study was casted using a vacuum induction furnace.
The cast steel was heated at 1150 °C for 2 h before hot forging.

processing_steps.reduction_ratio: forged to rods of section plane 35 mm × 70 mm × 100 mm
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot forged to rods with a section plane of 35 mm × 70 mm × 100 mm, followed by air cooling to room temperature.
The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h before hot rolling.

processing_steps.reduction_ratio: rolled to 3 mm thickness in 6 passes
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot rolled to 3 mm thick steel sheet through 6 passes; start rolling and finish rolling temperatures were 1150 °C and 850 °C, respectively.
The hot-rolled steel was subsequently water quenched to 550 °C.
After the water quench to 550 °C, the steel was air cooled to room temperature.
Solution treatment performed at 700–1000 °C for 1 h; the specimen solution treated at 700 °C is referred to as H70.
The solution treatment at 700 °C for 1 h was followed by water quenching.

structures.overall_structure: H70 consists of martensite and spheroidal M5C2-carbide formed by decomposition of nearly all the original austenite, with 12.2% austenite retained; M5C2-carbide is widely distributed both at δ-ferrite grain boundaries and among martensite laths; large δ-ferrite regions are present.

phases_present.morphology: formed from decomposed original austenite; martensite laths

precipitates.distribution: widely distributed both at δ-ferrite grain boundaries and among martensite laths

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: gauge width 12.5 mm; gauge length 50 mm; machined from the solution-treated sheets along the longitudinal direction
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: tensile test after 700 °C/1 h solution treatment + water quenching

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: True stress-strain curve of H70 (700 °C) in Fig. 2a; no yield point phenomenon; curve ends near a true strain of ~0.18 below the 1000 MPa gridline.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: phase-level microhardness used to distinguish the phases in the H70–H100 solution-treatment series

measurement_conditions.test_standard: densitometry based on the Archimedes Principle

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: secondary-electron imaging; H70 at Mag = 1.09 K X, WD = 8.7 mm, 10 µm scale bar
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe the microstructure of the solution-treated specimens (Fig. 1a for H70).
characterization_methods.key_findings: For H70 the SE-SEM micrograph shows large light-grey δ-ferrite regions, fine M5C2-carbide particles, and martensite regions.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: element distribution in austenite and ferrite
characterization_methods.purpose: Investigate the element distribution in austenite and ferrite (Mn and Al contents of austenite).
characterization_methods.key_findings: Mn and Al contents of austenite in H70 measured by EDS: Mn 8.91 mass%, Al 5.22 mass% (Table 4).

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: direct comparison method using (200)α and (211)α ferrite peaks and (220)γ and (311)γ austenite peaks
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the austenite volume fraction and measure the C content in austenite.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Retained austenite volume fraction of H70 = 12.2%; C content in austenite of H70 = 0.556 mass% (Table 4).

characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the density of the steel.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Density of the present steel is about 6.95 g/cm3, about 11% lower than pure Fe.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: bright-field TEM of region near fracture after tensile deformation
characterization_methods.purpose: Examine dislocation morphology in ferrite and martensite after tensile deformation.
characterization_methods.key_findings: High-density dislocations were observed in both ferrite and martensite; a small amount of austenite remained after the strong TRIP effect. (Measurement was performed on deformed tensile specimens.)

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: combined band contrast and phase identification maps; Schmid factor maps
characterization_methods.purpose: Distinguish ferrite/austenite/martensite grains, measure austenite volume fractions and Schmid factors during deformation.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Deformation-induced martensite transformation occurred continuously with increasing true strain; blocky austenite at ferrite triple junctions transformed first while lath-like austenite rotated. (EBSD analysis was carried out on the deformed specimen across true strains 0.03–0.27.)

computational_details.simulation_method: analytical empirical equations for martensitic transformation temperatures
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Composition of austenite in H70: C 0.556 mass%, Mn 8.91 mass%, Al 5.22 mass% (Table 4); elemental contents in mass percentage.

analytical_models.equation_role: Equation (2): Ms (°C) = 539 − 423C − 30.4Mn − 12.1Cr − 17.7Ni − 7.5Mo + 10Co − 7.3Si; used to calculate Ms from austenite composition
analytical_models.model_note: Calculated Ms for H70 = 33 °C (Table 4 and Section 4.2).

analytical_models.model_name: Md30 (temperature at which 50% of austenite transforms to martensite at true strain 30%)
analytical_models.equation_role: Equation (3): Md30 (°C) = 497 − 462(C+N) − 20Ni − 18.5Mo − 13.7Cr − 8.1Mn − 9.2Si; used to calculate Md30 from austenite composition
analytical_models.model_note: Table 4 lists Md30 = 168 °C for H70, whereas the text of Section 4.2 states Md30 = 268 °C for H70 (numerical inconsistency between table and text).

unmapped_findings: Austenite composition of H70 measured by XRD (C) and EDS (Mn, Al) is C 0.556 mass%, Mn 8.91 mass%, Al 5.22 mass% (Table 4).

Calculated transformation temperatures for H70: Ms = 33 °C; Md30 = 168 °C per Table 4, but the text of Section 4.2 states Md30 = 268 °C for H70 — a numerical inconsistency between the table and the text.
For H70 the austenite volume fraction decreased from 12.2% before deformation to 4.5% after tensile deformation, giving a martensite transformation ratio of 0.631 (Fig. 7b).
The high UTS of H70 was attributed to secondary phase and martensite strengthening, whereas its low TE was caused by the low austenite fraction.

H70 showed an obvious three-stage work-hardening behaviour; in Fig. 2b the 700 °C curve shows a small stage-2 (S2) hump near the ~2500 MPa level, and its true stress-strain curve ends near a true strain of ~0.18 (below the 1000 MPa gridline); no yield-point phenomenon occurred.
The density of the present steel (to which H70 belongs) is about 6.95 g/cm3, which is about 11% lower than pure iron.
